entries.summary: In 1145 a math book by Abraham bar Hiyya was translated into Latin, giving European scholars new ways to solve equations.
entries.why: The algebra taught in schools today grew from methods like these.
entries.origin: Barcelona / Italy; County of Barcelona / Italian city-states
entries.originator: Abraham bar Hiyya; Plato of Tivoli (translator)
entries.deepDive: In 1145 the Latin translation of a Hebrew book by Abraham bar Hiyya, a Jewish scholar in Barcelona, reached European readers. Called the Liber embadorum, it was the first work to bring the solution of quadratic equations into Latin mathematics. The Italian mathematician Fibonacci later built his own geometry book on it. The methods it carried are the ancestors of the equations students still solve in school today.

source.name: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, Plato of Tivoli (via Encyclopedia.com)

entries.summary: Maimonides, a doctor as well as a scholar, wrote a practical guide to diet and healthy living for a ruler in Egypt.
entries.why: Eat in moderation, stay active, prevent illness early: his advice still sounds modern.
entries.deepDive: In the 1190s Maimonides, the great Jewish scholar who served as personal physician to al-Afdal, the son of Saladin and ruler in Cairo, wrote him a health manual. Drawing on Galen and Hippocrates, it urged moderate eating, regular activity and preventing illness before it starts. It was translated into Hebrew in 1244 and later into Latin, bringing it to European readers. Researchers today still compare it with modern health guidance.

source.name: Rambam Maimonides Medical Journal, The Maimonides Model for a Regimen of Health (Segal and Blazer, 2020)

entries.summary: Gersonides described a simple measuring stick, the Jacob's staff, for finding the angle between stars.
entries.why: Sailors later used it to find their way at sea.
entries.deepDive: Gersonides, a Jewish scholar in southern France, described a simple tool for measuring the angle between two stars: a long staff with a crosspiece that slides along it. He explained it in his astronomy book, finished in 1328, and it became known as Jacob's staff. Light and easy to carry, it later served sailors on Portuguese and Spanish ships. A stick and a crosspiece helped people find their way across oceans.

source.name: Museo Galileo (Florence), Cross-Staff, Inventions database

entries.summary: Gersonides compared his predictions of where the planets would be with what he actually saw in the sky.
entries.why: Checking a theory against real observations is how science still works.
entries.deepDive: Gersonides did not simply trust the ancient astronomers. He measured the sky himself, using a pinhole device called a camera obscura, and compared his results with what Ptolemy's model predicted. Ptolemy's model said Mars should change in apparent size about sixfold; Gersonides found about twofold. He drew up his own astronomical tables and a new model of the heavens. Checking a theory against careful observation is how science still works.

source.name: Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers (Springer), Gersonides: Levi ben Gerson, via University of St Andrews

entries.summary: Abraham Zacuto's tables showed where the sun, moon and planets would be each day, and European navigators carried them on their voyages.
entries.why: They helped sailors work out where they were on the open ocean.
entries.deepDive: Abraham Zacuto, a Jewish astronomer who advised the king of Portugal, compiled tables of the movements of the heavenly bodies, so a navigator could look up where the sun would be on any day. His student Joseph Vizinho translated them into Latin, and they were printed in 1496 as the Almanach perpetuum. The tables prepared for Vasco da Gama's voyage to India were based on his work, and until 1537 Portuguese sun tables were computed from his figures.

source.name: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, Zacuto (via Encyclopedia.com)

entries.summary: Amatus Lusitanus reported tiny valves inside veins and suggested they help steer the flow of blood.
entries.why: It was a step toward understanding how blood circulates through the body.
entries.originator: Amatus Lusitanus (João Rodrigues de Castelo Branco)
entries.deepDive: In 1547 Amatus Lusitanus, a Portuguese-born Jewish doctor who taught anatomy in Ferrara, blew air into a vein while scholars watched. The air would not get past the tiny valve inside, which suggested that valves steer blood in one direction. He published the account in 1551. Historians still debate how well he understood circulation, but his careful experiment was an early step toward explaining how blood moves through the body.

source.name: Garrison-Morton (Jeremy Norman, History of Medicine), Rodrigues de Castelo Branco (Amatus Lusitanus)

entries.summary: In 1688 Joseph Penso de la Vega wrote the first book about stock trading, describing the booms and panics of the Amsterdam exchange.
entries.why: His picture of greedy and fearful investors still fits markets today.
entries.deepDive: In 1688 Joseph Penso de la Vega, a Jewish merchant and writer who had settled in Amsterdam, published Confusion de Confusiones. Written as conversations between a philosopher, a merchant and a shareholder, it is the first known book to describe how a stock exchange works, including puts, calls and market manipulation. He called the exchange an honest business but warned of its tricks, and said profits can turn to losses overnight. The book stayed little known until the 1890s.

source.name: Sotheby's, The First Book to Describe a Stock Exchange

entries.summary: Jacob Rodrigues Pereira taught deaf students to speak and to read lips, one pupil at a time.
entries.why: His methods helped shape special education.
entries.deepDive: Jacob Rodrigues Pereira was born into a Marrano family and returned to Judaism after his family settled in France. He taught deaf children to speak and to read lips, one pupil at a time. In 1746 he showed a deaf teenager who could say short phrases and answer simple questions. In 1749 he presented his work to the Paris Academy of Sciences and met King Louis XV, who gave him a yearly pension. Later teachers of the deaf built on his methods.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Judaica at Encyclopedia.com

entries.summary: Isaac de Pinto wrote one of the first serious studies of how government borrowing and credit move money through an economy.
entries.why: Countries still argue over the same questions of debt and credit.
entries.deepDive: In 1771 Isaac de Pinto, an Amsterdam banker and a main investor in the Dutch East India Company, published a treatise on circulation and credit. At a time when many feared public borrowing, he argued that public credit could make a country richer by putting more money into circulation. The book was translated into English in 1774. His interests also included Jewish emancipation. Countries still argue over the same questions about debt and credit.

source.name: The Historical Journal (Cambridge University Press), article on national debt and political obligation, DOI 10.1017/S0018246X21000832 (article title not visible in the extract)

entries.summary: Moses Mendelssohn argued that governments should never force anyone's religious beliefs.
entries.why: His case helped open the way to freedom of conscience and equal citizenship.
entries.deepDive: In 1783 the German Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn published Jerusalem, or On Religious Power and Judaism. He argued that the state and the church each have limits, and that neither may force anyone's beliefs: power should work by persuasion, not compulsion. Writing as a member of a religious minority, he made the case for freedom of conscience in the years before the French Revolution. His plea is still read as an early argument for religious liberty.

source.name: German History in Documents and Images (German Historical Institute), Mendelssohn, Jerusalem, or On Religious Power and Judaism (1783)

entries.summary: Abraham Stern built a machine that could do arithmetic and even find square roots.
entries.why: Machines began doing number work people once did by hand.
entries.deepDive: Abraham Stern grew up poor in the Polish town of Hrubieszów and trained as a watchmaker. The Polish nobleman and scientist Stanisław Staszic noticed his talent and helped him move to Warsaw. By 1817 Stern had built a calculating machine that could do the four basic operations and find square roots. He became the first Jewish member of Warsaw's Society of Friends of Science. Machines now do arithmetic that people once did by hand.

source.name: Engineering and Technology History Wiki (IEEE), Computing in Poland

entries.summary: Lewis Gompertz wrote one of the first books arguing that cruelty to animals is wrong and should be against the law.
entries.why: Animal-protection laws today rest on the same idea.
entries.deepDive: In 1824 Lewis Gompertz, an English inventor of Jewish family, published Moral Inquiries on the Situation of Man and of Brutes, a book whose full title calls cruelty to animals a crime. That same year he was among the founders of the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, later the RSPCA. In 1826 he helped raise the money that cleared its debts. Animal-protection groups today rest on the same idea.

source.name: The Canadian Encyclopedia, Humane Societies

entries.summary: Giacomo Meyerbeer's Robert le diable dazzled Paris in 1831 with huge sets, special effects and soaring music.
entries.why: Its spectacle became the model for opera houses across Europe.
entries.deepDive: On 21 November 1831 the Paris Opéra premiered Robert le diable by Giacomo Meyerbeer. He had first planned a smaller comic opera, then reworked it into a five-act spectacle with lavish staging and a story full of the supernatural. Audiences were wild for it: by 1893 it had been performed 751 times at the Opéra. Its blend of music and spectacle helped define grand opera.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Robert le Diable

entries.summary: Robert Remak found thin nerve fibers with no protective coating, an early step in mapping how the nervous system is wired.
entries.why: It is an early piece of the map doctors still use to understand nerves.
entries.deepDive: In 1836 Robert Remak, a young Jewish researcher in Berlin, published his first studies of the fine structure of nerves. His 1838 doctoral thesis described thin gray fibers with no protective coating, the myelin sheath, now called Remak's fibers. He also showed that the coated nerve fibers are not hollow tubes, as had been believed. These were early pieces of the map doctors still use to understand how nerves are wired.

source.name: Journal of Neurology via PubMed Central, Robert Remak (1815-1865), Grzybowski and Pietrzak, 2013

entries.summary: James Joseph Sylvester gave the matrix its name in 1850.
entries.why: Photo software, weather models and machine learning all lean on matrix math.
entries.deepDive: In 1850 the English mathematician James Joseph Sylvester used the word matrix for a rectangular block of numbers. He chose the Latin word for womb because he saw such a block as the place from which determinants arise. Within a year he had shared the idea with Arthur Cayley, who went on to study matrices in their own right. Photo software, weather models and machine learning all lean on this math today.

source.name: Nicholas Higham, Cayley, Sylvester, and Early Matrix Theory (University of Manchester, 2007)

entries.summary: Robert Remak showed that new cells come from existing cells splitting in two.
entries.why: Growth, healing and many diseases all start with cell division.
entries.deepDive: In 1852 Robert Remak, a Jewish physician and embryologist in Berlin, published what he had seen in frog eggs: one cell dividing into two, then four, and on from there. Some scientists, including Matthias Schleiden, had thought cells formed the way crystals do. Three years later Rudolf Virchow made the same idea famous with a Latin motto meaning every cell comes from a cell, without citing Remak. Growth and healing both rest on cell division.

source.name: Garrison-Morton (Jeremy Norman, History of Medicine), Remak, Robert, 1852 entry

entries.summary: Jewish charities in New York opened a hospital in 1855 that took in patients of every background.
entries.why: It grew into Mount Sinai, one of America's leading hospitals.
entries.originator: Founders of Jews’ Hospital in New York
entries.deepDive: In 1852 nine men representing Jewish charities in New York agreed to build a hospital for the city's poor Jews. The Jews' Hospital opened in 1855 with 45 beds on West 28th Street. At first it admitted Jewish patients and accident victims. During the Civil War it widened its doors, and in 1866 it dropped its sectarian charter and took the name Mount Sinai. A medical school followed in 1968.

source.name: Baron, The Mount Sinai Hospital: A brief history, Mount Sinai Journal of Medicine 67(1), 2000 (catalog abstract only; full text not opened)

entries.summary: Ferdinand Lassalle founded the first organized party for German workers in 1863.
entries.why: It gave working people an organized political voice.
entries.deepDive: On 23 May 1863 in Leipzig, the German socialist writer and organizer Ferdinand Lassalle founded the General German Workers' Association and was elected its president. He had urged working people to organize peacefully and to press for the right to vote. Lassalle died in 1864, but in 1875 his association merged with another workers' party to form the forerunner of today's Social Democratic Party of Germany. It gave working people an organized political voice.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ferdinand Lassalle

entries.summary: Your body's first responders: Julius Cohnheim watched white blood cells squeeze out of blood vessels into injured tissue to fight infection.
entries.why: It showed that inflammation is your body sending defenders to the injury.
entries.deepDive: In 1867 Julius Cohnheim, a young German pathologist working with Rudolf Virchow in Berlin, watched under a microscope as white blood cells slipped through the walls of tiny blood vessels in a frog's inflamed tissue and moved into the surrounding area. He showed that pus is made mostly of the remains of these cells. It was a breakthrough in understanding inflammation: the body sends its defenders to the spot.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Julius Friedrich Cohnheim

entries.summary: Ferdinand Cohn sorted bacteria into groups by how they look and behave.
entries.why: Naming and grouping germs made it possible to study and fight them.
entries.origin: Breslau (now Wrocław); Kingdom of Prussia / German Empire
entries.deepDive: In 1872 Ferdinand Cohn, a botanist from Breslau, published a study that sorted bacteria into groups by their shape: balls, rods, curved forms and spirals. Until then many scientists lumped these tiny organisms together. Cohn argued that bacteria are living things that can be arranged into genera and species, and his was the first systematic attempt to do it. His groups are still the basis of how bacteria are named. In 1876 he also helped launch Robert Koch's anthrax discovery.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ferdinand Cohn

entries.summary: Jacob Davis came up with copper rivets for work pants, and with Levi Strauss he patented them in 1873.
entries.why: Riveted work pants became blue jeans, worn around the world.
entries.deepDive: In 1872 Jacob Davis, a tailor in Reno, Nevada, wrote to the San Francisco merchant Levi Strauss with an idea: copper rivets at the points where work pants tore. Davis could not afford a patent on his own, so the two men applied together, and the patent was granted on 20 May 1873. Levi Strauss & Co. began making riveted work pants, the first blue jeans. Both men were Jewish immigrants, Davis from Riga and Strauss from Bavaria. Jeans are now worn in nearly every country.

source.name: Hagley Museum and Library

entries.summary: Camille Pissarro helped stage the first independent Impressionist exhibition, in Paris in 1874.
entries.why: Impressionism changed how the world paints and looks at art.
entries.deepDive: On 15 April 1874 about thirty artists opened an exhibition in Paris, in the former studio of the photographer Nadar. They had formed their own cooperative, the Société anonyme, because the official Salon kept turning them away. Camille Pissarro was among the artists who set it up and showed his landscapes there. The show was poorly received, and one critic used the word impressionist as an insult. The name stuck, and the artists in that room changed how people paint and see.

source.name: National Gallery of Art, press release on Paris 1874: The Impressionist Moment

entries.summary: Emile Berliner patented a better transmitter, the part of the phone you speak into.
entries.why: Phone calls became clear enough for everyday conversation.
entries.deepDive: In 1877 Emile Berliner, a young German-born inventor in Washington, DC, built a better transmitter for the new telephone, the part you speak into. His loose-contact design made the voice louder and clearer. He filed for a patent on 4 June 1877, and the Bell company bought his rights and hired him. Thomas Edison had filed a similar claim that spring, and the two collided in a long legal fight over credit. Either way, the improved microphone helped make phone calls clear enough for everyday use.

source.name: Encyclopedia.com, Emile Berliner

entries.summary: Paul Ehrlich used colored dyes to spot a new kind of cell, the mast cell, now known for its role in allergies.
entries.why: These cells store histamine, the chemical behind many allergic reactions.
entries.deepDive: As a medical student in the late 1870s, Paul Ehrlich was fascinated by colored dyes. Using them to stain tissue under the microscope, he spotted a new kind of cell packed with dark granules. In his 1878 doctoral thesis he named it the mast cell. His staining methods went on to help doctors tell different blood cells apart. Today we know that mast cells store histamine, a chemical the body releases in allergic reactions.

source.name: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, Ehrlich, Paul (via Encyclopedia.com)

entries.summary: James Joseph Sylvester founded the American Journal of Mathematics in 1878.
entries.why: American mathematicians finally had a major journal of their own.
entries.deepDive: In 1878 James Joseph Sylvester, an English mathematician then teaching at the new Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, founded the American Journal of Mathematics and served as its first editor. It was the first research journal in mathematics in the United States, giving American mathematicians a place to publish their work at home. Sylvester also introduced graduate study in mathematics to American universities and gave the whole field a boost.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, James Joseph Sylvester

entries.summary: Michael Reese's fortune built a Chicago hospital open to all, whatever their religion or nationality.
entries.why: Chicago gained a major charity hospital with its doors open to everyone.
entries.originator: Michael Reese’s heirs and Jewish philanthropic network
entries.deepDive: Michael Reese, a German Jewish immigrant who made his money in Chicago, died in 1878 and left funds toward a hospital. The United Hebrew Relief Association used them to build one, on the condition that it be named for him and treat all patients, whatever their race, religion or nationality. Michael Reese Hospital opened on 23 October 1881, and a nursing school followed in 1890. Historians note the promise of care for all took longer to keep. It became a major charity hospital.

source.name: University of Illinois Chicago, Mapping Care, Michael Reese Hospital School of Nursing

entries.summary: David Gestetner invented a stencil pen that let one master copy print page after page.
entries.why: Schools and offices could make copies quickly and cheaply.
entries.deepDive: In 1881 David Gestetner, a Hungarian-born immigrant in London, invented the Cyclostyle, a pen with a tiny toothed wheel that punched holes in waxed paper to make a stencil. Ink pushed through the holes, so one master could make copy after copy. His rotary design, patented in 1901, wrapped the stencil around a revolving drum so copies came out continuously. His company employed 6,000 people by his death in 1939.

source.name: Science Museum Group Collection, Gestetner's rotary cyclostyle no 6 duplicator

entries.summary: Emma Lazarus wrote the poem now linked to the Statue of Liberty, welcoming the world's tired and poor.
entries.why: Her words became America's promise to newcomers.
entries.deepDive: In 1883 the New York poet Emma Lazarus, whose family was Sephardic Jewish, was asked to write a sonnet for an art and literary auction raising money for the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty. Inspired by her work with refugees on Ward's Island, she wrote The New Colossus on 2 November 1883. It calls the statue the Mother of Exiles. Lazarus died in 1887, and in 1903 her words were placed on a plaque inside the pedestal. Her welcome to newcomers still defines the statue.

source.name: U.S. National Park Service, Emma Lazarus

entries.summary: Michael Marks opened a market stall in Leeds where everything cost one penny.
entries.why: His stall grew into Marks & Spencer and helped make clear, fixed prices normal in shops.
entries.deepDive: In 1884 Michael Marks, a Jewish refugee from Poland who had come to England a few years earlier, opened a stall in Leeds' Kirkgate Market. Its sign told shoppers there was no need to ask the price, because everything cost a penny. In 1894 he took on Thomas Spencer, a cashier, as his partner, and Marks & Spencer was born. That market stall grew into one of Britain's best-known clothing and food retailers.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Marks & Spencer PLC

entries.summary: Samuel Gompers became the first president of a new federation joining America's trade unions.
entries.why: The unions it led pushed for shorter hours, fair bargaining and better labor laws.
entries.originator: Samuel Gompers and participating trade unions
entries.deepDive: In December 1886 delegates from craft unions met in Columbus, Ohio, unhappy with the Knights of Labor, and formed the American Federation of Labor. They chose Samuel Gompers, a cigar maker born in London to a Dutch Jewish family, as president; he declined at first and accepted when nominated a second time. He led the federation for nearly forty years. It became the first lasting national labor union in the United States and gave working people an organized national voice.

source.name: The Clio, Samuel Gompers, labor leader and first president of the AFL

entries.summary: Bernard Sachs described a rare inherited disease of the nervous system in young children, now called Tay–Sachs.
entries.why: Knowing the disease made diagnosis possible, and later genetic testing.
entries.originator: Bernard Sachs; Warren Tay (earlier ophthalmologic observation)
entries.deepDive: In 1881 the English eye doctor Warren Tay noticed a cherry-colored spot in the retina of a sick infant. In 1887 the New York neurologist Bernard Sachs described the same illness in a two-year-old girl without knowing of Tay's report. Later he saw that it ran in families and named it amaurotic family idiocy. Doctors came to call it Tay-Sachs disease. A careful description and a name gave doctors a way to recognize a rare inherited illness and a first step toward understanding it.

source.name: Encyclopedia.com, Tay-Sachs and "Jewish" Diseases

entries.summary: In 1887 L. L. Zamenhof published Esperanto, a new language designed to be easy for anyone to learn.
entries.why: People around the world still use it as a shared second language.
entries.deepDive: In 1887 Ludwik Lejzer Zamenhof, an eye doctor in Warsaw, published a short book under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, meaning one who hopes. It set out a new language with simple, regular grammar, meant to be everyone's second language. Zamenhof grew up in Białystok, where Poles, Russians, Germans and Jews often could not understand one another, and he hoped a shared language would ease such divisions. The language took its name from his pen name and remains the most widely spoken invented language.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, L.L. Zamenhof

entries.summary: Emile Berliner traded Edison's cylinders for flat discs that could be copied by the thousands.
entries.why: Music could be recorded once and sold by the million.
entries.deepDive: Thomas Edison's phonograph, introduced in 1877, recorded sound on wax cylinders. In 1887 Emile Berliner applied for a patent on a flat-disc record and player, and in 1888 he introduced his first model. His discs were cut with a side-to-side groove and could be mass-produced from a master, so the same recording could be copied again and again, which was awkward and costly with cylinders. Berliner's flat records became the way the world listened to music.

source.name: Engineering and Technology History Wiki (IEEE), Gramophone

entries.summary: Louis Brandeis and Samuel Warren argued in 1890 that people have a right to be left alone.
entries.why: Modern privacy law, from intrusive media to personal data, builds on their argument.
entries.originator: Louis D. Brandeis and Samuel D. Warren
entries.deepDive: In December 1890 two Boston lawyers, Samuel Warren and Louis Brandeis, published an article in the Harvard Law Review titled The Right to Privacy. Alarmed that instant photographs and newspapers were intruding on private life, they argued that the law should protect a person's right to be let alone. The phrase came from an earlier legal writer, but they built it into a legal principle. Brandeis later became a Supreme Court justice. Legal scholars trace the legal idea of privacy to their article.

source.name: Arizona Law Review, Glancy, The Invention of the Right to Privacy (1979)

entries.summary: Gabriel Lippmann found a way to capture true colors in a photograph using light waves alone, without dyes.
entries.why: It won him the 1908 Nobel Prize in Physics.
entries.deepDive: In the 1890s the French physicist Gabriel Lippmann found a way to photograph color using the way light waves interact. A mirror behind the photographic plate reflected the light back through the emulsion, creating layers of tiny dark bands whose spacing matched the wavelengths of the colors in the scene. Those layers could then show the scene's colors as an image. The method never came into widespread use, but in 1908 it won him the Nobel Prize in Physics.

source.name: NobelPrize.org, Gabriel Lippmann, Facts (Nobel Prize in Physics 1908)

entries.summary: Waldemar Haffkine made an early vaccine against cholera and tested it on himself first.
entries.why: Vaccination became a practical way to protect people from cholera.
entries.deepDive: In 1892, working at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, Waldemar Haffkine made a cholera vaccine from weakened bacteria and tested it on animals. Before offering it to anyone else, he injected himself on 18 July 1892, using a dose four times stronger than later used, and carefully recorded his reactions. Field trials in India followed from 1893, and within two years tens of thousands of people had been inoculated. He is credited with the first effective vaccination against cholera.

source.name: James Lind Library, Hawgood, Waldemar Mordecai Haffkine: prophylactic vaccination against cholera and bubonic plague in British India

entries.summary: Nathan Straus paid to have milk pasteurized and set up stations where families could get safe milk.
entries.why: Fewer babies fell sick from germs in milk.
entries.deepDive: Nathan Straus, the co-owner of Macy's department store, believed pasteurized milk could stop babies from dying of diseases carried in raw milk. In 1892 he and his wife funded a laboratory for pasteurized milk, and in 1893 the first of his milk depots opened in Lower Manhattan, selling safe milk for a penny a glass and giving it to families who could not pay. By 1920 he had set up nearly 300 depots in 36 American cities. His crusade helped make pasteurized milk the norm.

source.name: Columbia University, Sheffield Farms project, Chapter 5: Community Actions

entries.summary: Julius Wolff showed that bones reshape themselves to handle the loads placed on them.
entries.why: Doctors still use his idea that bones adapt to the loads placed on them.
entries.deepDive: In 1892 the Berlin surgeon Julius Wolff published The Law of Bone Transformation after years of studying cut sections of bone. He found that the spongy inside of a bone is built as a regular lattice of tiny struts that cross at right angles, and that when the way a bone is used changes, its inner structure and outer shape change to match. His idea that bone adapts to mechanical stress became a foundation of orthopedics, the care of bones and joints.

source.name: Clinical Orthopaedics and Related Research (Springer), on Julius Wolff

entries.summary: Lillian Wald started a service of nurses who visited poor families at home in New York.
entries.why: Community nursing became a regular part of public health.
entries.deepDive: In the autumn of 1893 Lillian Wald, a young nurse, left medical school with her friend Mary Brewster and moved into a poor immigrant neighborhood on New York's Lower East Side, offering her services as a visiting nurse. In the first months they visited over 125 families. Her service grew into the Henry Street Settlement, and in 1902 a Henry Street nurse in a public school led New York to start the world's first citywide school nursing program. Community nursing became a regular part of public health.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Lillian D. Wald

entries.summary: Émile Durkheim studied how splitting work into specialized jobs changes the bonds between people.
entries.why: His ideas still help explain modern jobs and society.
entries.deepDive: In 1893 the French sociologist Émile Durkheim published The Division of Labour in Society, his doctoral thesis. He asked what holds a society together when people no longer do the same work. In small traditional communities, he argued, people are bound by being alike; in modern societies, by depending on one another's specialized jobs, a bond he called organic solidarity. He warned that this works only when the work is fairly regulated and suits the person doing it.

source.name: Charles University (Prague), course reading on Durkheim's The Division of Labor in Society

entries.summary: Émile Durkheim laid out rules for studying society with evidence, the way scientists study nature.
entries.why: Sociology became a research field of its own.
entries.deepDive: In 1895 Émile Durkheim, a French scholar born into a Jewish family in Épinal, published The Rules of Sociological Method. He argued that society could be studied scientifically by treating social facts, such as laws, customs and shared beliefs, as things that shape individuals from outside. That same year he set up the first sociology department in Europe and became France's first professor of sociology.

source.name: Wikipedia, Émile Durkheim

entries.summary: Sigmund Freud and Josef Breuer published cases of patients who talked through painful memories with their doctor.
entries.why: Talk-based therapy, much changed since, began here.
entries.deepDive: From 1880 the Viennese physician Josef Breuer treated a young woman known in print as Anna O., later identified as Bertha Pappenheim. She found that her symptoms eased when she talked through where they began, and she called this the talking cure. In 1895 Breuer and Sigmund Freud published Studies on Hysteria, the first detailed account of free association, which is usually treated as the starting point of psychoanalysis.

source.name: Jeremy Norman's History of Information, The Origin of Psychoanalysis

entries.summary: Jacques Hadamard proved a rule for how often prime numbers appear as numbers grow larger.
entries.why: Prime numbers later became the base of public-key encryption.
entries.deepDive: In 1896 the French mathematician Jacques Hadamard and the Belgian Charles de la Vallée Poussin, working separately, proved the prime number theorem. It says how thinly prime numbers are spread: the count of primes up to x is roughly x divided by the natural logarithm of x. Legendre and Gauss had guessed this a century earlier. Primes later became the base of RSA encryption, invented in 1977, but that use came long after Hadamard.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, prime number theorem

entries.summary: Fernand Widal devised a blood test to tell whether a patient had typhoid fever.
entries.why: Lab tests became a standard way to diagnose infections.
entries.deepDive: In June 1896 the French physician Fernand Widal showed that blood serum from a typhoid patient makes typhoid bacteria clump together. Doctors could now test for the disease in its early stage, instead of guessing from symptoms. He built on the clumping work of Gruber and Durham. The Widal test is still used in some places, though a single result can mislead because other infections can cause false readings.

source.name: PubMed Central, Hoke, The Serum Diagnosis of Typhoid Fever (1898)

entries.summary: During a plague epidemic in India, Waldemar Haffkine made and tested an early vaccine against plague.
entries.why: It gave doctors one of the first tools against plague outbreaks.
entries.deepDive: Waldemar Haffkine, a Jewish bacteriologist born in Odesa, was sent to Bombay when plague broke out in October 1896. Working in a tiny laboratory at Grant Medical College, he prepared a plague vaccine from pure cultures. At its first trial, in a Bombay prison in January 1897, 2 of 147 inoculated prisoners caught plague and none died, against 12 cases and 6 deaths among 172 who were not inoculated.

source.name: Nature, Waldemar Mordecai Haffkine (1959)

entries.summary: Paul Ehrlich gave one of the first explanations of how the body makes antibodies to fight poisons and germs.
entries.why: It laid groundwork for today's vaccines and antibody medicines.
entries.deepDive: In 1897 Paul Ehrlich proposed that cells carry side chains on their surface that lock onto toxins, and that the body answers an attack by making extra side chains that float free in the blood as antitoxins. It was one of the first explanations of how antibodies work. Ehrlich shared the 1908 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Élie Metchnikoff for their work on immunity. His idea that a chemical could be built to hit a single target, a magic bullet, led to the first modern drug against syphilis.

source.name: Neue Deutsche Biographie (Deutsche Biographie), Ehrlich, Paul

entries.summary: Émile Durkheim used population records to show that suicide rates rise and fall with social conditions.
entries.why: It showed that social conditions shape personal lives, and that data can reveal how.
entries.deepDive: In 1897 Émile Durkheim published Suicide, a study of suicide rates across populations, including Catholic and Protestant communities. He used statistics to argue that rates differ with the strength of social ties and are not only a matter of individual psychology. The book is treated as an early model of quantitative social research and helped separate sociology from psychology and political philosophy.

source.name: Wikipedia, Émile Durkheim

entries.summary: In 1899 Sigmund Freud's The Interpretation of Dreams argued that dreams reveal hidden thoughts.
entries.why: It shaped how people think and talk about the unconscious mind.
entries.deepDive: Sigmund Freud's Die Traumdeutung, The Interpretation of Dreams, argued that dreams carry meaning and offer a way into the unconscious mind. It reached readers in November 1899, though the title page says 1900. The first printing was only 600 copies and took eight years to sell. Seven more editions followed in Freud's lifetime, and the book became the best known of his works.

source.name: Library of Congress, Die Traumdeutung (Sigmund Freud Collection)

entries.summary: Lillian Wald helped bring nurses into New York's public schools to care for children and keep them in class.
entries.why: School nurses are now part of education systems in many countries.
entries.originator: Lillian Wald and Henry Street nurse Lina Rogers, with the New York City Board of Health
entries.deepDive: In October 1902 Lillian Wald, who founded the Henry Street Settlement, sent her nurse Lina Rogers into four New York City schools. Until then sick children were simply sent home. Rogers treated common problems at school, visited families and sent children back to class. The trial was extended and 27 more nurses were hired that year. Reports of how far absence fell vary by source, so no figure is given here.

source.name: University of Virginia School of Nursing, Flashback Friday: Lina Rogers, first school nurse

entries.summary: Albert Einstein showed that mass and energy are two forms of the same thing.
entries.why: It showed that a little matter holds enormous energy, an idea behind atomic energy.
entries.deepDive: In September 1905 Albert Einstein published a short paper asking whether the inertia of a body depends on its energy content. It carried the equation E = mc2: mass and energy are equivalent. Because the speed of light squared is a huge number, a tiny amount of matter corresponds to a vast amount of energy. Decades later this idea helped explain and develop atomic energy.

source.name: Gresham College, Einstein's Annus Mirabilis, 1905

entries.summary: Albert Einstein explained how light knocks electrons out of metal, showing that light comes in tiny packets of energy.
entries.why: It helped found quantum physics and the light sensors in modern devices.
entries.deepDive: In March 1905 Albert Einstein proposed that light comes in tiny packets of energy, later called photons. This explained the photoelectric effect, in which light knocks electrons out of metal, something the wave theory of light could not do. He thought it the most revolutionary of his 1905 papers because it pushed forward the young quantum theory. It won him the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics.

source.name: Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics, Marking Einstein's Annus Mirabilis

entries.summary: Albert Einstein showed that time and space depend on how fast you are moving.
entries.why: It changed how physicists think about time and space.
entries.deepDive: In June 1905 Albert Einstein published his special theory of relativity. Assuming that the speed of light is the same for every observer, he showed that space and time are not fixed: lengths can contract and time can slow for something moving relative to an observer. It replaced the Newtonian idea of absolute time. The follow-up paper gave E = mc2.

source.name: Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics, Marking Einstein's Annus Mirabilis

entries.summary: Paul Ehrlich's lab, with Sahachiro Hata, made Salvarsan, a chemical designed to kill the germ that causes syphilis.
entries.why: It was one of the first modern targeted drugs.
entries.originator: Paul Ehrlich laboratory and Sahachiro Hata
entries.deepDive: Paul Ehrlich's Frankfurt laboratory hunted for a chemical that would kill the syphilis microbe without killing the patient. Compound 606 had been set aside as useless until Ehrlich asked his Japanese assistant, Sahachiro Hata, to repeat the tests in 1909. Marketed in 1910 as Salvarsan, it reached some 20,000 patients within the year. Before it, mercury was the usual treatment. Ehrlich later improved it as Neosalvarsan.

source.name: PubMed Central, Salvarsan history article

entries.summary: Max Factor created a thin makeup that looked natural under the bright lights and cameras of early films.
entries.why: Film makeup moved from stage paint to a look made for the camera.
entries.deepDive: Max Factor, a Jewish cosmetics maker who settled in Los Angeles, saw that the thick greasepaint used on stage looked terrible on film. In 1914 he created a thinner, translucent greasepaint in cream form, sold in twelve shades. It was flexible and light and did not crack under studio lights, unlike stick greasepaint from the stage, and it became the standard makeup in Hollywood.

source.name: EBSCO Research Starters, Max Factor

entries.summary: Albert Einstein explained gravity as the bending of space and time.
entries.why: It predicted how light bends around stars and how gravity slows time.
entries.deepDive: In November 1915 Albert Einstein presented the field equations of general relativity, a theory that describes gravity as the bending of space and time. It explained an oddity in the orbit of Mercury. In 1919 eclipse observations at Sobral in Brazil and Príncipe off West Africa showed starlight bent by the Sun as predicted, and made him world famous. GPS satellites also need relativity corrections to keep accurate time.

source.name: arXiv, The 1919 eclipse results which verified General Relativity and their later detractors

entries.summary: Max Factor matched makeup shades to each person's skin, hair and eye color.
entries.why: Choosing makeup by your own coloring became the norm.
entries.deepDive: In 1918 Max Factor released Color Harmony, a range of face powders in several shades chosen to match a person's skin, hair and eye colour. It let him give each film actor a consistent, custom look under the lights. The idea of matching makeup to colouring moved from the studio to the shop, where it is still used today. Some sources date the Color Harmony idea to 1920.

source.name: ASU FIDM Museum, Max Factor and Hollywood

entries.summary: Emmy Noether proved that every smooth symmetry in nature comes with something that is conserved, such as energy.
entries.why: Physicists use it to find the basic laws of the universe.
entries.deepDive: In 1918 Emmy Noether, working in Göttingen, proved that every continuous symmetry of a physical system gives a conserved quantity. Because the laws of physics are the same at any time, energy is conserved; because they are the same in any place, momentum is conserved. She took up the problem to help Hilbert and Klein with puzzles in general relativity. Her theorem underlies the Standard Model of particle physics.

source.name: arXiv, Colloquium: A Century of Noether's Theorem

entries.summary: Sigmund Freud described the mind as three parts: the id, the ego and the superego.
entries.why: Words like ego entered everyday speech.
entries.deepDive: In The Ego and the Id, published in 1923, Sigmund Freud divided the mind into three parts. The id holds raw drives, the super-ego holds internalized rules and conscience, and the ego mediates between them and the outside world. This structural model replaced his earlier map of conscious, preconscious and unconscious. Freud took the word id from the physician Georg Groddeck. Parts of the model have drawn strong criticism.

source.name: Freud Museum Vienna, Freud's dynamic structural model

entries.summary: George Gershwin blended jazz with a full orchestra in his 1924 Rhapsody in Blue.
entries.why: It brought jazz into the concert hall.
entries.deepDive: George Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue premiered on 12 February 1924 at Aeolian Hall in New York, in bandleader Paul Whiteman's concert An Experiment in Modern Music, with Gershwin at the piano. It was one of the first successful works to blend jazz and classical music. Its success led Whiteman to repeat the concert the next month at Aeolian Hall and two months later at Carnegie Hall. Ferde Grofé orchestrated the original.

source.name: Library of Congress, Rhapsody in Blue at 100

entries.summary: The Jazz Singer, made by Warner Bros. in 1927, was a major film with recorded songs and spoken lines.
entries.why: It began the move from silent films to sound.
entries.originator: Warner Bros. Jewish founding family and production team
entries.deepDive: On 6 October 1927 Warner Bros. released The Jazz Singer, with Al Jolson, the first feature-length film with synchronized dialogue. Only the songs and a few spoken scenes were recorded, about a quarter of the film. It used Vitaphone, a sound-on-disc system Warner had bought and first used in 1926. The film's success made Warner Bros. a major studio and earned it a special Academy Award. The four Warner brothers began as theater owners in Pennsylvania.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, The Jazz Singer (film 1927)

entries.summary: Chaim Weizmann and the Sieff family opened a science institute in 1934 that later became the Weizmann Institute.
entries.why: It grew into a major center for scientific research.
entries.originator: Chaim Weizmann and Sieff family backers
entries.deepDive: In 1934 Chaim Weizmann, a chemist and later Israel's first president, founded a research institute in Rehovot, fourteen years before the State of Israel existed. It was first called the Daniel Sieff Research Institute, for the son of its London backers, Israel and Rebecca Sieff, and was renamed the Weizmann Institute of Science in 1949. Today it offers only postgraduate degrees in the natural and exact sciences.

source.name: Wikipedia, Weizmann Institute of Science

entries.summary: Simcha Blass found a way to water crops one drop at a time, right at the roots.
entries.why: Farms in dry places grow more food with far less water.
entries.deepDive: Simcha Blass, a water engineer, developed a dripper that releases water drop by drop at the roots of plants, using friction to slow the flow. In 1965 he and Kibbutz Hatzerim in the Negev founded Netafim, Hebrew for drops, and in 1966 the company produced the first commercial dripper. Drip irrigation uses far less water than flooding a field, and it now helps farmers in dry regions around the world grow more food with less water.

source.name: MIT Sloan Management Review, "To Conserve Water for Agriculture, a Solution from the Desert"

entries.summary: Abraham Lempel and Jacob Ziv found a way to shrink computer files without losing a single bit.
entries.why: It is behind smaller files and faster downloads on almost every device.
entries.deepDive: In 1977 Jacob Ziv and Abraham Lempel, engineers from the Technion in Haifa, published a method for squeezing data into less space. It replaces each repeated stretch of data with a short pointer back to where the same stretch first appeared, and it needs no advance knowledge of the data. Versions of the method, known as LZ77 and LZ78, sit inside ZIP files, GIF and PNG images and much of the data sent across the internet. IEEE named the Lempel–Ziv algorithm a Milestone in 2004.

source.name: IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 23(3), 1977 (Ziv and Lempel)

entries.summary: Aaron Ciechanover and Avram Hershko, with Irwin Rose, found how cells tag worn-out proteins for disposal.
entries.why: It won the 2004 Nobel Prize and helps explain cancer and other diseases.
entries.originator: Aaron Ciechanover, Avram Hershko and Irwin Rose
entries.deepDive: At the start of the 1980s Aaron Ciechanover and Avram Hershko of the Technion in Haifa, working with Irwin Rose in Philadelphia, found how cells get rid of proteins they no longer need. A small protein called ubiquitin is attached as a label, and the tagged protein is sent to the cell's disposal unit, the proteasome, to be broken down. The process controls cell division, DNA repair and parts of the immune defense. When it fails, people fall ill. The three shared the 2004 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

source.name: NobelPrize.org, Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2004 press release

entries.summary: Dan Shechtman found crystals with a pattern that never repeats, something textbooks said was impossible.
entries.why: It won the 2011 Nobel Prize and changed the definition of a crystal.
entries.deepDive: On 8 April 1982 Dan Shechtman, a materials scientist from the Technion working at the US National Bureau of Standards, saw an electron diffraction pattern that textbooks said was impossible: a crystal with a regular order that never repeats. For years many scientists rejected the finding. Other groups made quasicrystals by 1987, and the discovery changed how scientists define a crystal. Shechtman received the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

source.name: NobelPrize.org, Dan Shechtman facts

entries.summary: Gil Shwed, Marius Nacht and Shlomo Kramer founded Check Point and built a firewall that tracks every connection.
entries.why: Firewalls like it are a basic defense on business networks.
entries.originator: Gil Shwed, Marius Nacht and Shlomo Kramer
entries.deepDive: Gil Shwed first developed the idea for what became FireWall-1 in April 1993 and started Check Point Software that July with two friends. FireWall-1 was unveiled at the 1994 NetWorld+Interop show and used stateful inspection, which tracks each network connection and lets through only traffic that belongs to a known one. It was not the first firewall, but it created the mass market for them.

source.name: Computerworld, It's been 20 years since Check Point FireWall-1 made firewalls mainstream

entries.summary: Israeli company VocalTec released Internet Phone in 1995, software that let people talk over the internet.
entries.why: Calling over the internet, now routine, started here.
entries.deepDive: Alon Cohen and Lior Haramaty, two veterans of the Israeli army's telecommunications wing, founded VocalTec. In February 1995 it released Internet Phone, widely described as the first voice-over-IP software. You could simply download it, with no extra hardware. Its base was their patented Audio Transceiver, which smoothed out the delays of sending speech in packets. Rival services came later, and early users could only call others on the same service.

source.name: IEEE Spectrum, Voice Over IP: Setting Phone Service Free

entries.summary: In 1996 the US FDA approved glatiramer acetate, developed at the Weizmann Institute, to treat multiple sclerosis.
entries.why: Patients gained a new drug that reduces relapses.
entries.origin: Rehovot, Israel / United States; Israel / United States
entries.originator: Weizmann Institute research team and Teva Pharmaceuticals
entries.deepDive: In the late 1960s Weizmann Institute scientists Ruth Arnon, Michael Sela and Dvora Teitelbaum set out to make synthetic molecules that could provoke an immune response. They ended up with copolymer-1, a copy of a protein from the nerve sheath, and a new way of treating multiple sclerosis. Teva ran a trial at 11 US medical centers, and in December 1996 the FDA approved Copaxone for relapsing-remitting MS.

source.name: Science News, New multiple sclerosis drug clears hurdle (28 September 1996)

entries.summary: In 1996 the Israeli company Mirabilis released ICQ, letting people see when friends were online and message them instantly.
entries.why: Every chat app since follows the pattern it set.
entries.deepDive: In 1996 a small Israeli company, Mirabilis, released ICQ, short for I seek you. It let people see when friends were online and send them messages instantly, and it became the first widely used instant-messaging service on the internet. AOL bought Mirabilis in 1998. ICQ set the pattern for the chat and messaging apps that followed.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica, ICQ

entries.summary: Sergey Brin and Larry Page ranked web pages by the links pointing to them.
entries.why: Searching the web became how the world finds information.
entries.origin: Stanford / Menlo Park, California; United States
entries.deepDive: Sergey Brin, born in Moscow, and Larry Page met at Stanford and began a search project in 1996, first called BackRub. It ranked a web page by the pages linking to it, in effect treating links as votes. The method became PageRank, named for Page, and the two founded Google in 1998. The patent belongs to Stanford University, which licensed it to Google. Brin and Page share the credit.

source.name: Lemelson-MIT, Sergey Brin and Larry Page

entries.summary: A camera the size of a vitamin pill photographs the gut from the inside.
entries.why: Doctors can see deep inside the intestines without a tube.
entries.deepDive: In 1981 Gavriel Iddan, an engineer at Rafael, Israel's defense research agency, met an Israeli gastroenterologist, Eitan Scapa, during a year in Boston and learned that much of the small intestine was out of reach of a doctor's scope. Iddan spent years designing a camera small enough to swallow. Given Imaging, founded in 1998, built it, and in 2001 the US Food and Drug Administration cleared the capsule, later sold as PillCam. Patients swallow it like a pill, and it photographs the gut on its way through.

source.name: Annals of Translational Medicine (PMC), "The history of time for capsule endoscopy"

entries.summary: Amnon Shashua and Ziv Aviram founded Mobileye to teach cars to spot hazards with a single camera.
entries.why: Its camera systems help cars warn drivers of danger.
entries.originator: Amnon Shashua and Ziv Aviram / Mobileye
entries.deepDive: In 1999 Hebrew University professor Amnon Shashua and businessman Ziv Aviram founded Mobileye in Jerusalem. The idea began on a car ride, when Shashua said a camera could give a collision warning, since a person with one working eye can still judge depth. Mobileye's software detects vehicles using only a camera and a processor. In March 2017 Intel announced a $15.3 billion takeover, the largest purchase of an Israeli company to that date.

source.name: Wikipedia, Mobileye

entries.summary: Dov Moran's M-Systems brought out DiskOnKey, an early USB flash drive.
entries.why: Carrying files in your pocket became easy.
entries.deepDive: In April 1999 Amir Ban, Dov Moran and Oron Ogdan of the Israeli company M-Systems filed a patent for a flash disk that plugs into a computer's USB port. Sold with IBM from 2000 as DiskOnKey, it held 8 megabytes and quickly replaced the floppy disk. The credit is contested: Singapore's Trek 2000 showed its ThumbDrive in early 2000, and China's Netac holds competing patents. M-Systems filed first; Trek showed first.

source.name: Engineering and Technology History Wiki, Dov Moran

entries.summary: Ada Yonath mapped the ribosome, the cell's protein factory, atom by atom.
entries.why: It shows how antibiotics work and won her the 2009 Nobel Prize.
entries.originator: Ada Yonath and Weizmann Institute collaborators
entries.deepDive: The ribosome is the cell's protein factory, built from hundreds of thousands of atoms. In the 1970s Ada Yonath of the Weizmann Institute set out to map it with X-ray crystallography, a goal many thought impossible. In 2000 she and other researchers completed the structure. The maps show how many antibiotics attack bacterial ribosomes, which helps in designing new drugs. Yonath shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

source.name: NobelPrize.org, Ada E. Yonath facts

entries.summary: Mark Zuckerberg and his college friends launched Facebook for students in 2004.
entries.why: It changed how people stay in touch.
entries.deepDive: In early 2004 Harvard sophomore Mark Zuckerberg launched thefacebook.com with fellow students Eduardo Saverin, Dustin Moskovitz and Chris Hughes. It began as a site for Harvard students and quickly grew, and the team later moved operations to Palo Alto. Its origin is disputed. Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss and Divya Narendra accused Zuckerberg of taking their idea, and the two sides settled. Saverin left in 2005 and settled his own dispute in 2009.

source.name: Fox Business, How Facebook was founded

entries.summary: Waze turns drivers into traffic reporters, so the app can steer everyone around jams, crashes and roadwork.
entries.why: Millions of drivers save time because other drivers share what they see.
entries.originator: Ehud Shabtai, Amir Shinar and Uri Levine / Waze
entries.deepDive: In 2006 Israeli programmer Ehud Shabtai started FreeMap Israel, a community project to build a free digital map of Israel. In 2008 he, Amir Shinar and Uri Levine turned it into a company that became Waze, a navigation app fed by drivers' own reports of traffic and road conditions. Google bought Waze in June 2013 for about $1.3 billion. It then had nearly 50 million users, and its development team stayed in Israel.

source.name: Wikipedia, Waze
